body:
From limited political activity to participation by ordinary people

Before Gandhi emerged as a major Indian leader, nationalist politics already included petitions, public meetings, the Swadeshi movement and boycotts. Gandhi helped turn resistance into a form of collective action in which peasants, workers, students, traders and women could participate. Their grievances were different, but a specific, understandable demand could bring them into a common campaign.

Gandhi developed satyagraha during struggles against racial discrimination in South Africa, beginning in 1906, and returned to India in January 1915. His early Indian interventions addressed particular problems: indigo cultivators in Champaran, land-revenue demands in Kheda and the grievances of Ahmedabad textile workers. These were concrete disputes, not abstract declarations of independence.

What made a campaign Gandhian in practice?

Satyagraha was active, disciplined, nonviolent resistance to a perceived injustice. Participants organised meetings, explained their demand, sought public support and used a suitable form of nonviolent protest. They were expected not to retaliate violently even when they faced arrest or repression. Gandhi also used negotiation and compromise when they could redress the grievance.

Success was not automatic. Local people could have different expectations of a movement, and large gatherings were difficult to keep nonviolent. That is why Gandhi treated preparation and self-discipline as important parts of mass action.

Historical distinction: Satyagraha is an active method of resisting injustice without physical violence; it is not simply doing nothing or accepting a wrong.

Gandhi's underlying ideas, Hind Swaraj (1909) and the 11 vows belong to the separate study of Gandhian thought; here the focus is their historical use.

Prelims focus

  • Gandhi returned to India from South Africa in January 1915.
  • Major early Indian campaigns: Champaran (1917), Kheda (1918) and Ahmedabad mill workers (1918).
  • Satyagraha required nonviolent action and discipline, not passivity.
  • Trap: A protest does not become Gandhian merely because it invokes Gandhi's name.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts–III, Class 8, ch. 9, "The Making of the National Movement: 1870s–1947," printed pp. 115–119; NCERT, India and the Contemporary World–II, Class 10, "Nationalism in India," sec. 1.1; Gandhi Smriti and Darshan Samiti, "Chronology of Mahatma Gandhi," entries for 1906, 1915 and 1917–1918 (consulted 21 November 2026).]

title: How Gandhian Mass Action Worked in the Freedom Struggle

body:
The common requirement: nonviolence

Gandhian political action took different forms according to the immediate wrong being challenged. The common requirement was organised public participation without attacks on people or property. A peaceful procession, a boycott and the deliberate breach of an unjust law were therefore not identical acts, even when all were used in the wider practice of satyagraha.

Distinguish the forms by what participants actually did

FormImmediate actionTextbook example
Peaceful protest or hartalDemonstrate, hold meetings or suspend normal activity to oppose a measure.Nationwide hartal against the Rowlatt Act on 6 April 1919.
Non-cooperationWithdraw voluntary support from colonial institutions, honours or goods.Surrender British titles, leave government schools or boycott foreign cloth in 1920–1922.
Civil disobedienceOpenly and nonviolently break a particular unjust law and accept the risk of punishment.Break the colonial salt law at Dandi on 6 April 1930.

Boycott and picketing are not the same act

A boycott means refusing to buy, use or participate in something. Refusing to purchase imported cloth was a boycott. Picketing means demonstrating at or near a shop or institution to persuade others not to patronise it; picketing of liquor shops was one example. A picket remains consistent with Gandhi's method only when it is peaceful; intimidation and assault are not required or permitted by the nonviolent method.

Why the difference matters

A student leaving a government college during Non-Cooperation withdrew cooperation; the act did not itself break a salt law. A person making salt in defiance of the government's monopoly deliberately disobeyed a law. Both could serve the nationalist movement, but the immediate form of resistance differs.

Voluntary suffering or acceptance of arrest did not mean that violence was acceptable if a crowd became angry. Gandhi held that a satyagrahi should refrain from violent retaliation.

Prelims focus

  • Hartal: collective suspension of activity; Rowlatt protest, 6 April 1919.
  • Non-cooperation: withdrawal of support, such as boycott of foreign goods or government institutions.
  • Civil disobedience: deliberate nonviolent breach of an unjust law; salt law, 6 April 1930.
  • Trap: A boycott need not involve breaking a law, whereas the Dandi action did.

[Sources: NCERT, India and the Contemporary World–II, Class 10, "Nationalism in India," secs. 1.1–1.3 and 3.1; NCERT, Our Pasts–III, Class 8, ch. 9, printed pp. 116–121; M. K. Gandhi, Constructive Programme: Its Meaning and Place, "Place of Civil Disobedience," revised foreword dated 13 November 1945 (online edition consulted 21 November 2026).]

pictures.alt: All forms require disciplined nonviolence: non-cooperation withdraws support, civil disobedience breaks a specific law, and hartal suspends activity.
pictures.caption: Different nonviolent acts challenged authority in different ways.

title: The Main Methods: Protest, Non-Cooperation and Civil Disobedience

body:
Champaran, Bihar: indigo cultivators in 1917

In Champaran (1917), indigo cultivators faced oppressive plantation arrangements. Gandhi investigated their conditions and supported their grievances. The campaign demonstrated that gathering facts about a local injustice, refusing to be silenced and rallying affected people could become an effective form of political action. Its immediate concern was relief for cultivators, not a general boycott of all government institutions.

Kheda, Gujarat: land revenue in 1918

In Kheda (1918), crop failure left many cultivators unable to meet land-revenue demands. Gandhi supported a nonviolent campaign for suspension or relaxation of collection from distressed peasants. Vallabhbhai Patel helped organise cultivators in Gujarat. A central form of resistance was the withholding of land revenue while villagers maintained collective discipline. The immediate aim was relief from an unaffordable revenue demand.

Ahmedabad, Gujarat: a labour dispute in 1918

The Ahmedabad textile-mill dispute (1918) concerned the wages of mill workers. Gandhi supported their strike and sought a fair settlement between workers and mill owners; the dispute was ultimately resolved through arbitration. The campaign shows that satyagraha could be used in an industrial labour dispute as well as in an agricultural one. Gandhi also fasted during the strike as part of his effort to maintain workers' resolve.

Compare the immediate grievance

Champaran involved indigo cultivation; Kheda involved land revenue after crop failure; Ahmedabad involved industrial wages. They belong together because Gandhi used nonviolent organisation to address identifiable grievances, but their social groups and demands should not be interchanged.

Prelims focus

  • 1917—Champaran, Bihar: indigo cultivators and plantation grievances.
  • 1918—Kheda, Gujarat: crop distress and land-revenue relief; Vallabhbhai Patel assisted organisation.
  • 1918—Ahmedabad, Gujarat: textile workers and a wage dispute.
  • Trap: Kheda was a peasants' revenue satyagraha, not an Ahmedabad factory strike.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts–III, Class 8, ch. 9, printed pp. 115–119; Gandhi Heritage Portal, "Mahatma Gandhi Events Chronology," Champaran 1917 and Kheda 1918 entries; Gandhi Heritage Portal, "Chronology: Event Detail Page," entries for Ahmedabad, 14 February–18 March 1918 and Kheda, 22 March 1918 (web chronology consulted 21 November 2026).]

pictures.caption: Kheda linked a specific rural hardship to collective, disciplined resistance.

title: Champaran, Kheda and Ahmedabad: Local Satyagraha in Action

body:
Rowlatt Satyagraha: protest against restrictive legislation

The Rowlatt Act (1919) gave the colonial authorities sweeping powers over political activity, including detention without trial. Gandhi called for a nonviolent nationwide hartal on 6 April 1919. Processions and stoppages spread the protest beyond a local dispute. Violence and harsh repression followed in some places; Gandhi withdrew the satyagraha as the situation escalated. The immediate issue was the Act and the curtailment of civil liberties.

Non-Cooperation: withdrawing everyday support

The Non-Cooperation Movement began in January 1921. It sought wider participation through refusal of colonial titles, schools, councils and foreign goods. Wearing khadi and boycotting foreign cloth connected a political movement to the everyday choice of what to wear and buy. Students, traders, peasants and other groups joined for different reasons; participation was broad but not uniform.

Following the violent Chauri Chaura incident on 4 February 1922, in which a crowd set fire to a police station, Gandhi called off the movement. This decision illustrates his insistence that a mass campaign must remain nonviolent. It should not be confused with the earlier Rowlatt satyagraha.

Salt Satyagraha: a simple issue that could unite people

Salt was used by both wealthy and poor households. Gandhi therefore chose the colonial salt tax and government monopoly as an easily understood grievance. On 12 March 1930, he began the march from Sabarmati Ashram with 78 volunteers. At Dandi in Gujarat on 6 April 1930, he deliberately broke the salt law, turning the march into a central example of civil disobedience. Making or collecting salt against the law was different from merely refusing to buy imported cloth.

Prelims focus

  • Rowlatt Act: 1919; nationwide hartal on 6 April 1919.
  • Non-Cooperation: began January 1921; withdrawn after Chauri Chaura in February 1922.
  • Salt March: departed Sabarmati on 12 March 1930 with 78 volunteers; salt law broken at Dandi on 6 April 1930.
  • Trap: Foreign-cloth boycott is an example of non-cooperation; breaking the salt law is civil disobedience.

[Sources: NCERT, India and the Contemporary World–II, Class 10, "Nationalism in India," secs. 1.2, 1.3, 2.1 and 3.1; NCERT, Our Pasts–III, Class 8, ch. 9, printed pp. 116–122; Gandhi Heritage Portal, "Mahatma Gandhi Events Chronology," entries for 1919, 1922 and 1930 (consulted 21 November 2026).]

pictures.alt: Men and women in traditional 1930s dress peacefully collect salt with bowls and baskets beside shallow coastal waters at Dandi.
pictures.caption: Salt made an unjust law visible in the daily lives of ordinary people.

pictures.alt: Salt united rich and poor against colonial control, leading from Sabarmati on 12 March 1930 with 78 volunteers to law-breaking at Dandi on 6 April.
pictures.caption: In 1930 a familiar household necessity became the subject of deliberate law-breaking.

title: National Mobilisation: The Rowlatt Protest, Non-Cooperation and Salt Satyagraha
